title: WHEN HOLINESS IS TWISTED INTO LEGALISM
paragraphs: WHEN HOLINESS IS TWISTED INTO LEGALISM

The rules looked holy. The people sounded biblical. But somewhere between “be holy” and “prove that you are holy,” Jesus was pushed to the edge—and exhausted believers learned to fear people more than they loved Christ.
There is a kind of Christianity that can make you afraid to breathe wrong.
You know what I mean.
You walk into the room and immediately start checking yourself.
Is my clothing acceptable?
Did I say the wrong thing?
Will they question my salvation because of what I watched?
Will they think I am rebellious because I asked why?
Did I pray long enough?
Did I fast enough?
Did I read enough chapters today?
Did I look spiritual enough?
And beneath all those questions is one terrifying question you may never say out loud:
“Is God disappointed in me again?”
That question has followed some believers for years.
They love Jesus.
They genuinely want holiness.
They hate their sin. They repent when they fall. They want their lives to honor God.
But somehow their relationship with God has become an endless spiritual courtroom where the verdict never seems settled.
There is always another standard.
Another unwritten expectation.
Another person to impress.
Another failure to remember.
Another reason to wonder whether God has finally had enough.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing about this kind of bondage is that it often arrives wearing the clothes of holiness.
That is why we need to talk about legalism.
Not because holiness is outdated.
Not because obedience does not matter.
Not because grace gives us permission to sin.
It does not.

Scripture commands holiness. Peter writes, “Be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16, echoing Leviticus 11:44–45). Jesus calls His disciples to obedience. Paul repeatedly warns believers against sexual immorality, greed, idolatry, drunkenness, hatred, deception, and the works of the flesh. The New Testament never presents grace as permission to make peace with sin.
The Gospel does something far more radical.
Grace forgives the sinner and then begins transforming the sinner.
So legalism is not the same thing as taking holiness seriously.
That distinction matters.

Legalism appears when human performance, rule-keeping, religious identity, or man-made standards begin doing work that belongs to Christ alone—or when human traditions are elevated until they function as though God Himself commanded them.
And Jesus confronted that danger with frightening clarity.
In Mark 7:8, He told religious leaders:
“You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men.”
The Greek text is piercing:
ἀφέντες τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ κρατεῖτε τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
aphentes tēn entolēn tou theou krateite tēn paradosin tōn anthrōpōn.
The force of the sentence is difficult to escape.
They were letting go of God’s command while holding tightly to human tradition.
Think about how terrifying that is.
You can become so determined to defend what you believe protects holiness that you eventually protect your system more fiercely than you protect what God actually said.
And you may never notice.
Because legalism rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I want to replace Jesus.”
It says:
“I just want Christians to take God seriously.”
That sounds noble.
Sometimes it is noble.
But then something changes.
Biblical commands become mixed with personal convictions.
Personal convictions become community expectations.
Community expectations become measurements of spirituality.
Measurements become judgments.
Judgments become identity.
And eventually someone who breaks your rule is treated as though they broke God’s Word—even when God never gave the rule.
That is where something beautiful becomes distorted.
A Christian may personally decide not to drink alcohol at all. That conviction may be wise and deeply beneficial.
Another may establish strict boundaries around entertainment.
Another may choose particular clothing because of conscience and modesty.
Another may avoid certain social environments.
Another may fast regularly.
Another may observe particular devotional disciplines.
There can be wisdom, self-control, sacrifice, and sincere worship in such decisions.
The danger begins when I quietly move from:
“I believe this is wise for me before God”
to:
“Everyone who truly loves God must do exactly what I do.”
Then comes the comparison.
“I would never wear that.”
“I would never listen to that.”
“A real Christian wouldn't go there.”
“If she were truly godly…”
“If he were really saved…”
And suddenly the cross is still hanging on the wall, but another measuring stick has entered the room.
This is why legalism can be so intoxicating.
It gives us something measurable.
Grace forces me to admit I am completely dependent upon Jesus.
Legalism gives me a scoreboard.
And scoreboards make comparison easy.
I prayed longer.
I dress better.
I know more Scripture.
I never miss church.
I don't watch what they watch.
I don't struggle with what he struggles with.
My children behave better.
My theology is cleaner.
My ministry is bigger.
My convictions are stricter.
And without realizing it, we can use holiness—the very thing that should make us more like Jesus—as material for pride.
Then somebody falls.
A hidden addiction comes into the light.
A marriage breaks.
A pastor confesses.
A young believer admits sexual sin.
Someone says, “I'm struggling.”
And instead of running toward the wounded with truth and grace, everybody moves backward.
Whispers begin.
Screenshots circulate.
People stare.
Someone who desperately needed restoration learns a devastating lesson:
Never let Christians see you bleeding.
So next time they hide.
They worship while hiding.
Serve while hiding.
Preach while hiding.
Smile while hiding.
Post Bible verses while hiding.
And every Sunday they walk into church carrying something they are terrified to confess because they have learned that looking holy is safer than becoming whole.
But Jesus never called us to perform righteousness for an audience.
He called us to Himself.
This does not mean churches should stop confronting sin.
Exactly the opposite.
A church ruled by grace can confront sin more honestly because grace removes the need to pretend sin isn't there.
Biblical grace says:
“Yes, this is sin.”
“Yes, it matters.”
“Yes, repentance is necessary.”
And then grace points to a bloodstained cross and says:
“And there is mercy here.”
Legalism says, “Clean yourself so you can come close.”
The Gospel says Christ came near while we were sinners, and His grace now teaches us to leave the life that was destroying us.
Paul captures this beautifully in Titus 2:11–12: the grace of God brings salvation and trains believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Do you see it?
Grace is not the enemy of holiness.
Grace trains us in holiness.
Real grace does not merely pardon rebellion and abandon us inside it.
Grace changes what we love.
Grace teaches us to say no.
Grace makes repentance possible.
Grace gives us the Holy Spirit.
Grace keeps bringing us back to Jesus until obedience begins growing not merely from terror of punishment, but from love for the One who saved us.
Jesus said:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15).
Notice the order of the relationship.
Love and obedience belong together.
But obedience is not a ladder by which sinners climb high enough to make Jesus save them.
Christ saves.
Then saved people learn to follow their Savior.
That difference changes everything.
Maybe nobody ever explained it to you that way.
Maybe you spent years believing God loved the polished version of you.
The disciplined version.
The church version.
The version who never doubted.
Never stumbled.
Never got angry.
Never became exhausted.
Never admitted temptation.
So every time you failed, you ran from God.
You promised Him you would do better.
You punished yourself emotionally.
You waited until you felt sufficiently ashamed.
Then you slowly started praying again.
But listen carefully.
Your shame was never your Savior.
Your religious performance was never your Savior.
Your denomination was never your Savior.
Your pastor was never your Savior.
Your reputation was never your Savior.
Your ability to keep everybody's expectations was never your Savior.
Jesus Christ is.
And Paul wrote something astonishing to believers being pressured toward religious bondage:
τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ἡμᾶς Χριστὸς ἠλευθέρωσεν
tē eleutheria hēmas Christos ēleutherōsen.
“For freedom Christ has set us free.”
Then:
στήκετε οὖν
stēkete oun.
“Therefore, stand firm.”
And finally the warning:
καὶ μὴ πάλιν ζυγῷ δουλείας ἐνέχεσθε.
Do not become entangled again in a yoke of slavery.
Even the Syriac Peshitta preserves the same striking image:
ܩܘܡܘ ܗܟܝܠ ܒܚܐܪܘܬܐ ܗܝ ܕܡܫܝܚܐ ܚܪܪܢ
Christ has liberated His people, and they are called to stand in that freedom.
But Christian freedom must never be confused with moral lawlessness.
Paul immediately guards against that misunderstanding later in Galatians 5:13: freedom is not an opportunity for the flesh; believers are to serve one another through love.
So the choice is not:
Legalism or sin.
The biblical alternative is far more beautiful:
Life in the Spirit.
There is a holiness produced by fear of people.
And there is a holiness produced by love for Christ.
From a distance they may occasionally look similar.
Both people may say no to temptation.
Both may attend church.
Both may read Scripture.
Both may live disciplined lives.
But underneath, two completely different hearts may be beating.
One says:
“I must do this so God will finally accept me.”
The other says:
“God has received me through Christ, therefore I want my life to belong completely to Him.”
One is trying to purchase what cannot be purchased.
The other is responding to what Christ purchased with His blood.
That is why the cross destroys both rebellion and religious pride.
At Calvary, the openly broken sinner cannot boast.
But neither can the respectable religious person.
Everybody comes empty-handed.
The addict.
The preacher.
The adulterer.
The lifelong church member.
The prodigal.
The theologian.
The prisoner.
The worship leader.
The woman everybody judged.
The man everybody admired.
At the foot of the cross, nobody gets to say:
“Jesus needed to die slightly less for me.”
Our confidence before God rests in Christ.
His righteousness.
His sacrifice.
His resurrection.
His mercy.
And when that truth finally reaches the places where legalism wounded you, something begins to change.
You stop obeying merely because you're terrified somebody will catch you.
You start wanting holiness because sin crucified the One you love and because His ways are good.
You stop asking:
“How much can I get away with?”
Grace never taught you that question.
Instead you begin asking:
“Jesus, what would please You?”
And perhaps for the first time, holiness becomes beautiful again.
Not cosmetic holiness.
Not Instagram holiness.
Not denominational holiness.
Not “everybody thinks I'm spiritual” holiness.
The kind born from union with Christ and the work of the Holy Spirit.
The kind that tells the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
The kind that forgives when bitterness feels justified.
The kind that confesses hidden sin.
The kind that shuts the door on pornography when nobody is watching.
The kind that refuses gossip even when everyone else calls it “concern.”
The kind that treats poor people with dignity.
The kind that loves enemies.
The kind that cares about justice, mercy, faithfulness, purity, humility, generosity, integrity, and truth.
The kind that looks increasingly like Jesus.
Because here is another uncomfortable possibility:
You can be extremely strict about things God barely addressed while becoming strangely casual about things He repeatedly commanded.
Jesus rebuked religious leaders for meticulously attending to smaller matters while neglecting “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (Matthew 23:23).
He did not condemn obedience. In fact, He said the proper response was not to neglect either.
He condemned distorted priorities.
And that warning still reaches us.
What if someone never misses a church service but destroys people with gossip?
What if someone dresses modestly but secretly despises everyone who dresses differently?
What if someone knows biblical doctrine but humiliates their spouse?
What if someone refuses certain entertainment but has no compassion for the suffering?
What if someone posts Scripture every morning but refuses to forgive?
External discipline can be valuable.
But external discipline cannot substitute for a heart being transformed by Jesus.
Somebody reading this has been exhausted for a very long time.
Not exhausted with Jesus.
Exhausted with trying to prove you deserve Him.
And maybe tonight the hardest thing for you to believe is also the simplest truth of the Gospel:
You never could deserve Him.
Neither could I.
That is why grace is grace.
Christ did not come because good people needed congratulations.
He came because sinners needed resurrection.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we fixed everything.
Not after our record improved.
While we were sinners.
And if you have been hiding because you failed again, hear this without twisting it into permission to remain in sin:
Come home.
Repent.
Tell Jesus the truth.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
Stop defending it.
Stop hiding it.
Bring it into the light.
But do not imagine that beating yourself bloody with shame can accomplish what the blood of Jesus accomplished at Calvary.
Turn to Christ.
Confess.
Receive mercy.
And walk forward in obedience.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs to become painfully simple:

“Jesus, I have spent years trying to look holy while hiding what is broken inside me. Forgive me. Save me from my sin and from my pride. Teach me holiness without hypocrisy, conviction without condemnation, obedience without self-righteousness, and freedom without compromise. Make me more like You.”
If something in this article exposed a place you have been hiding, don't turn the moment into another performance.
Be honest.
Someone else may read those words tonight and realize they are not the only believer struggling their way back toward the light.
Not as a superstition. Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
But financial support can be one practical way to help Gospel-centered resources reach more people when it is given freely and sincerely.
Not to make your name bigger.
Not to prove your spirituality.
But because somewhere behind another glowing screen may be a person who has spent twenty years believing Christianity means pretending they never bleed.
Let them discover Jesus.
Let them discover repentance without despair.
Holiness without hypocrisy.
Conviction without hopelessness.
Grace without compromise.
Freedom without rebellion.
And a Savior strong enough to confront their sin without crushing the sinner who comes to Him.
Because perhaps the greatest scandal of grace is this:
The people who finally understand holiness are often the people who have stopped pretending they never needed mercy.
And when Jesus gets hold of a life like that…
the mask can come off.
The hiding can end.
The chains can fall.
The sinner can repent.
The wounded can begin healing.
The proud can kneel.
And holiness can stop being a costume and become the fruit of a heart that belongs to Christ.
You were never called to become impressive enough to need less of Jesus; you were called to come close enough to discover that you will need Him forever.
